title: The solar dryer trial
paragraphs: A food-science club built two small solar dryers to help a neighbourhood cooperative preserve sliced bananas during humid weeks. One dryer had a clear cover; the other used a dark metal roof. The students wanted to compare drying time without changing the thickness of the fruit.

Farah and Jun prepared equal trays. They weighed them before placing one tray in each dryer. They also recorded cloud cover every hour. Jun noticed that the dark-roofed dryer became hot quickly, but he warned that this alone did not show which design removed more water.

After the first afternoon, the clear-covered dryer had lost more mass. This result surprised the group because its air temperature had often been lower. Farah suggested that the clear cover might allow steadier airflow, and the club added paper streamers near both vents to observe it.

The streamers moved more consistently in the clear-covered dryer. That pattern supported Farah's explanation, although the students knew that one day of data was not enough. The devices were left in place for four more trials under different cloud conditions.

Across all five trials, the clear-covered dryer usually removed water faster. The cooperative adopted that design for a larger prototype, but it kept the dark-roofed model for comparison. This allowed later groups to test whether the advantage remained during the dry season.
